findings.original:
> [!warning] Radix sort is not magic O(n)
> d is not a constant in general. To give n items distinct keys you need at least log_b(n) digits, so for distinct keys radix sort is O(n log n / log b) in disguise. It wins in practice because each step is a cheap array index rather than an unpredictable branch, and because real keys have a fixed width (32 or 64 bits) much smaller than "log n digits in base 2".
findings.correction:
> [!warning] Radix sort depends on key width
> The bound is O(d(n + b)) under constant-cost digit operations. Distinct keys require d ≥ ceil(log_b n), but that lower bound on d does not imply an upper bound: keys can be much wider. Fixed 32- or 64-bit keys give a fixed number of passes, with at most 2^32 or 2^64 distinct values. Python arbitrary-size integer division has its own bit cost.
findings.reason: Correct reversed bound and impossible key-width comparison.

findings.original: It is not stable by default
findings.correction: Stability depends on the MSD implementation; in-place variants may be unstable
findings.reason: MSD can be implemented stably.

findings.original: This makes radix sort work on floats too.
findings.correction: For non-NaN IEEE binary values this maps numerical order to unsigned-key order. Specify NaN placement and whether -0.0 and +0.0 must be treated as equivalent; simple bit transforms alone do not establish that policy.
findings.reason: Float total order needs special-value semantics.

findings.original: If all values fall in `[0.50, 0.51)`, they all land in one bucket and the cost is whatever the inner sort costs on n elements: O(n²) with insertion sort.
findings.correction: If all values fall in one interval of width 1/n aligned with a bucket, one bucket receives all n values. Insertion sort there can cost O(n²); the shown Python version uses sorted(), so its worst-case bound is O(n log n). A fixed-width interval such as [0.50, 0.51) spans many buckets when n is large.
findings.reason: Bucket width scales with n; code uses a different inner sort.

findings.reason: Independence supports expected occupancy second moment analysis.
